title: I Beat an IM!!!
transcript: I cannot believe that I'm about to say this, but today I defeated an international master in a game of chess. This is actually crazy, and I did it from my London system. I will never stop playing this opening. My opponent played a Benoni setup, which is one of the most annoying ways to counter the London. But out of the opening, I was defending myself pretty well. Although I did go wrong pretty quickly, allowing him to start an initiative on my king with F5. Now, I castled short, and so it makes sense for my opponent to put pressure on this king. I tried to avoid the opening of the lines, but unfortunately, my opponent manages to break through and bring a knight closer to my king. And now this bishop and this queen are also going to start participating in the attack. But I keep playing, and most importantly, I keep up on the clock. We have the same amount of time, but now, after just a couple more moves, my opponent finds this brilliant move, knight takes G3. The idea is that after I take this knight, he's going to play queen to G5 check. And after this check, unfortunately, I cannot cover with my queen because after this trade, my rook is going to hang. So here, I have to accept that I lost a pawn, and my opponent has a pretty significant advantage. But in the spirit of the fools will resign, I keep playing on, and I keep playing fast. Now, after all these trades, it is going to be pretty simple for my opponent to break through. Or at least, that's what I thought. But my opponent starts taking quite some time for his moves. He picks up another pawn on the edge of the board, and with less than 50 seconds on the clock, he starts to make the clock bleed. Whereas I am just trying to survive on the board and not lose on time. Here he manages to find a way to come in with the rook. But again, I defend my knight. Yes, you can take here with check, but after my king moves, what are you trying to do? I am in front of these pawns, and it's not that easy to push. Of course, black is completely winning, but you have to be able to win with 14 seconds on the clock. And at this point, I started to feel confident. 14 seconds, how is he going to checkmate me in 14 seconds? And not only that, for some reason, my opponent takes an entire 8 seconds to play this move. He was probably looking for some kind of plan. I just make sure that there's no checkmate. I move my king, and after a couple of moves, I win on time. And before you tell me that this is not an actual win, remember that the clock is a fundamental part of the game of chess. Chess is, after all, a game of efficiency. So I will take this W and add an international master to the roster of titled players that I've won against.
